profile.behavior: Forages for seeds and insects on the ground and among grass stems, often clinging to seed heads. Breeding males perform low, fluttering song flights; outside the nesting season, Bobolinks are social and often travel or feed in flocks.
field_marks: Compact songbird with a large, somewhat flat head and short neck.
Short, sharply pointed bill; pinkish in female and nonbreeding plumages, darker in breeding males.
Breeding male is black below and on the face, with a white back, shoulders, and rump plus a straw-colored nape.
Female and nonbreeding plumages are warm buff-brown with bold dark crown stripes, a dark eyeline, and streaked back and flanks.
Pointed wings and a short, rounded, multi-pointed tail.
Dark eyes and slender pinkish legs and feet.
profile.habitat: Tall grasslands, uncut pastures, overgrown fields, meadows, and prairies; also marshes and agricultural fields during molt and migration.

findings: The primary specimen is identifiable as an adult breeding male Bobolink: black face and underparts, extensive white back/shoulder/rump area, and a straw-colored nape agree with the attached male references and direct source descriptions.
The compact, large-headed, short-necked proportions and short, sharply pointed dark bill are species-appropriate. Both depicted heads have complete, consistent bills and visible dark eyes.

The primary specimen has one head, one beak, one tail, two attached legs, and two feet. The far-side wing is naturally hidden by the side-profile pose; the visible folded wing attaches convincingly. The crossed feet are visually crowded but remain traceable as two separate feet rather than duplicated or broken anatomy.
The detached spread-wing and head illustrations read as intentional supplementary studies, are not attached to the primary specimen, and show plausible Bobolink feather structure and head anatomy.
The tail is rounded and multi-pointed, the wings are pointed, and the slender pinkish legs agree with the proposed field marks and references.

All visible identification, measurement, habitat, behavior, and field-mark text is legible, correctly spelled, and matches the proposed wording and numbers. The repeated BODY LENGTH line agrees with the main length statement.

The printed sex-specific measurements exactly match Audubon's direct Bobolink account. Cornell currently publishes broader combined-sex values, while Animal Diversity Web gives averages that fall within the plate's ranges; this source variation does not establish a two-domain conflict with the proposed profile.

The vertical length diagram is internally consistent: 6.3 in (16 cm) is at the bottom, 7.1 in (18 cm) is at the top, values increase upward, and the nearby SCHEMATIC—NOT TO SCALE label prevents it from implying that the printed bird is life-size.

The habitat and behavior claims agree with Cornell and Audubon descriptions of tall grasslands, fields, marshes during migration, ground and grass-stem foraging, fluttering display flights, and flocking outside nesting.
No place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, or local-observation detail appears.
